Its back split with a wet tearing sound, and two wings snapped open — wings of raw flesh, bloated and veined, glistening like muscle pulled from the butcher's block. Black light poured down from them, and it wasn't light at all, not really — it was pressure, a dome of cold weight, like being submerged in black oil. Everyone inside it felt themselves compressed, gathered, packaged into a single point.

"The Malevolent Star guides, souls return to position — DECREED!"

Amid Chen Daji's stream of cursing, the whole company vanished the same way Xu Fu had — whoosh, and gone.

At that same moment, in the inner court of Mo City, Fan Ju felt the change in the Daoist Cache. He blinked, lips parting — then his eyes sharpened like a blade drawn from its sheath, and the corners of his mouth tried to climb. He pressed his lips together. His jaw went stiff with the effort of not laughing out loud.

He thought: Hahaha. The timing is MINE.

With the upheaval coming all at once, the Young General was not going to have time to succeed as the next Grand Master.

But Fan Ju was nowhere near stupid enough to say that aloud. Otherwise Qin Guxi would turn on him and pin him here by force, right to the floor of this city.

So instead he rose slowly from his seat and bowed, deep and respectful, to the Mohist Grand Master.

"This junior had many questions he longed to put to you, Elder. But with the dragon vein wandering and the world in upheaval, I must leave with my regrets."

"Elder Qin — until we meet again."

Qin Guxi had already felt Chen Daji's departure, and he was sulking about it — the Grand Master of the Mohists, a pillar of the old cosmic order, quietly resentful that a teenager had left without a proper goodbye.

So his answer came out flat, almost bored, barely attending.

"Fine. Fine."

"When the Daoist Cache opens again, I hope to discuss the diplomat's art with Chancellor Fan."

Fan Ju bowed lower still, and faded out of the inner court a piece at a time, like ink lifting from paper.

Hua Jiunan, his heart still with Chen Daji and Chang Baye, had just opened his mouth to go find them when Qin Guxi sighed and spoke first.

"Crown Prince, no haste. They are already gone from Mo City, under the Celestial Hound's escort."

"This is the Grand Master's Token. When you return to the mortal world — the Great Thousand World — give it to the Young General."

"Tell him: the day the Cache opens again is the day he becomes Grand Master."

Hua Jiunan was happy for Chen Daji, truly happy, and at the same time he received the Mohist token with both hands raised to his chest, fingers spread, in the posture of a courtier accepting an imperial decree — his face calm and ceremonial, his eyes warm.

"On behalf of Big Brother Daji, this junior thanks the Grand Master for his recognition."

"With the earth dragon rolling over and the Cache adrift, if there is nothing else you would command, this junior must also take his leave."

Qin Guxi understood perfectly how dire the situation was. He marveled — here was a boy with everything collapsing around him, and he stood steady as a rock, every inch a prince — and raised his hand in a gesture of invitation.

"You are too courteous, Crown Prince. I will see you out myself."

B.title: 第1236章 阴阳岛，飞来峰
B.text:
Chang Baye was already the fastest thing under heaven, and now, bathed in the cheering applause of the four heads of the Loiterers' Legion, he ran faster than he'd ever run in his life — legs blurring into a smear beneath him, air peeling off his flanks in visible waves, his whole enormous body vibrating with the joy of being admired.

But those four heads were not equal in rank.

The top three rode on the Eighth Master's back. Only Fourth Xin was wrapped in the great tail, carried like a child in a sling, the thick muscle of it gripping him with casual, unbothered strength.

The grand warden didn't feel a bit of shame about it, either.

This was a man who stood shoulder-to-shoulder with the emperor — the Emperor's Equal of the Lineage of the Perfected, and Lord of Ten Thousand Snakes besides. Ordinary spirits would beg for the honor of being carried like this, and he wouldn't deign to notice them.

Guided by Granny Hemp-Mourning's senses, the party tore along for nearly a hundred kilometers.

Then Chen Daji, who had been cooing at Little Diplomas to keep him calm, suddenly spoke up.

"Boss, boss — this place looks awful familiar."

"Ain't this where we met Sea Uncle? Only the island's gone — that big turtle done carted it off!"

Hua Jiunan looked hard, and by God, he was right.

A hundred-battle general in his past life, Hua Jiunan thought. Most souls needed only a thimbleful of Granny Meng's Tea of Forgetfulness to lose everything. Chen Daji had drunk half a vat — and his sense of space hadn't lost a step.

As they were talking, thick fog came boiling up out of the ground all around them.

It rose the way steam rises off the sea floor — cold, wet, briny, smelling of something dead and pickled in salt. In the space of a breath the world beyond ten feet simply stopped existing. Hua Jiunan couldn't see his own feet.

"Holy shit, it's haunted!"

That Chen fellow's head snapped left and right, hunting. He had one small dream in life, after all — catch himself a ghost and raise it like a pet.

Granny Hemp-Mourning cackled around her pipe stem.

"Heh-heh-heh, you little wretch, are you simple?"

"With our grandmother-and-grandson here, what ghost in its right mind comes calling to die?"

"You been drinking too much of that fake liquor!"

At that, the grand warden, still wrapped in the great tail, sheepishly lowered the bottle in his hand.

The label was peeling at one corner, the font all wrong, and printed across it in proud letters: CHRYsanthemum Village. The liquid inside was too clear. The cap was plastic, not cork. A sour, chemical-sweet smell washed over the whole party.

"Sacred God of Blessed Rest, ma'am, you don't understand — fake liquor gives me a splitting headache, but it's cheap."

"That old wretch who drove the car clean robbed me blind. I only just finished paying off what I owed, after the Little Master paid me for that funeral-crying gig over at Old Man Liu's..."

Seeing the grand warden looking so wounded, Granny Hemp-Mourning softened a little.

"That was this old woman's neglect. I've been a poor host."

"When we get back, I'll send General Xin home with some of the Ten-Fruit Wine I've had cellared on Hemp-Mourning Mountain these hundred years. Sip it slow."

The grand warden thanked her a thousand times, ten thousand ways. But Hua Jiunan had caught on the words *drove the car* — and thought immediately of Mo Huang.

Was it that one again — that wandering trickster god who treats the mortal world as his game board — who had "tricked" Granny Hemp-Mourning into coming to Yuhang?

In all the world, Hua Jiunan could think of no one else idle enough — and powerful enough — to make the Underworld itself cooperate in an operation.

The Ink Emperor's schemes looked shapeless, near to play. But there was meaning behind every one of them.

What, exactly, did he want with her?

He was still turning it over when a wind came through — not cold like weather. Cold like the presence of the dead. It didn't bite the skin; it sank through skin and muscle and settled in the marrow, and it carried the smell of wet stone and old salt.

Then Sea God Island appeared ahead of them, bit by bit.

It came the way a reflection comes up through the surface of a mirror — first a faint outline, then thickening, gaining weight, becoming real. Nothing ought to arrive that way.

And the island was wrong. All the living green was gone. The vegetation hung blackened and curled inward, like paper after a fire. The grey-green haze of death-qi clung to its slopes like mold on bread, and the sky directly above it was a bruised, darker color than the sky around it. The water at its edge didn't move. No waves. Nothing.

"Oh no. Oh, hell no — Yin-Yang Island?!"

Xin Lianshan, giddy with promised wine not a minute before, went rigid.

"Say, uh, Young General — I just remembered I gotta go home and shave my legs..."

The grand warden wanted to bolt. But the Eighth Master's tail still had him snug, and there was nowhere to go. So he just turned his big, innocent eyes on Hua Jiunan, pitiful as a whipped dog.

Hua Jiunan was the Emperor of Devotion, but he was no fool.

At a moment like this, you did not release your old horse that knew the road — though calling the centipede-king a horse was perhaps unkind. He coughed, pretended entirely not to understand the plea, and asked, all smiles:

"General Xin — what's a Yin-Yang Island? Tell me all about it, would you?"

Xin Lianshan would babble nonsense at Chen Daji all day, but he wouldn't dare show Hua Jiunan a hair of disrespect. He gathered himself and explained.

"Little Master, you ain't broken through the Veil of the Womb yet — the fog of your past life still blocks your memory, so a lot of the eerie stuff don't come back to you."

"A Yin-Yang Island is a place that drifts between the worlds of the living and the dead... The legendary immortal lands beyond the sea — the Three Isles and Ten Continents — they're all this kind of thing."

At that, the Child Ghost frowned its pale silver eyebrows and slowly shook its head.

"The Three Isles and Ten Continents were never immortal lands. Not at first. They were the Flown-Here Peaks."

"Only after our Lineage of the Perfected joined with the lineage of the Patchwork God and *purified* them did the so-called immortals move in and claim them."

"If we hadn't — those 'immortals' wouldn't have dared come within a hundred miles!!"

B.title: 第1798章 你俩给我等着
B.text:
Cornered with no way out, Chen Fu's voice shook.

"Look here, General Xin — if it were just me, I'd let you kill me and not lift a finger to stop you. But the children... they're still so small..."

The warden, for all his bulk, had a careful streak. He worried Master Chen might get the wrong idea and make his life hell later — so he hurried to explain, sweat beading on his thick neck, eyes darting to check whether the old man looked angry.

"Master Chen, rest easy — I've never once had a crooked thought about those little ghosts!"

"You and the two boys just stand back and watch. I'll hold out as long as I can hold out."

"And if it comes to the worst — worst case, we all die together! The Little Master and the Young General will avenge us no matter what!"

That was the speech. What the warden was actually thinking, as it turned out, was this:

If this godforsaken Bone Arena finishes me off, I might get invested as a god by Radiant Lady Guanghua. Bad luck turns into a promotion. Not bad.

But if I lay a hand on Master Chen myself... invested as a god? Invested as a pile of shit, more like.

Even if I rotted down to a ghost's ghost — the thing even ghosts are afraid of — the Young General would still find a way to haul me back up and make me suffer three hundred and sixty different ways.

So the choice is clear. I'm not stupid.

While the warden fought for his life against the sixteen-headed bone beast that had just torn its way into the fight, Zhao Fei and Zhang Chao were not idle either.

Zhao Fei leaned close to Zhang Chao's ear and whispered.

"Chao'er — get your relative out of that coffin, fast! Nobody's holding it down anymore!"

He didn't need to say it. Zhang Chao had been working at it the whole time.

Behold this man: teeth gritted, big face the color of a boiled shrimp, straining like a fellow who's been on the toilet forty minutes with nothing to show for it.

"Boss Zhao, I know! It's just — it's so close, it almost comes out and then it doesn't!"

"Blood! The thing in the coffin needs blood! It's just short! Just a little more!"

"Blood?" That one stumped even Zhao Fei.

If he hadn't been trapped inside the Bone Arena, he'd have knocked his own head open on the coffin lid to make up the difference. But now...

At that exact moment, a fat, bloated crow — round and heavy as a garbage-heap bird, wings beating with a dry papery rattle — caught the smell of death rising from below and began circling lower and lower over their heads.

Zhao Fei's big eyes rolled. He had an idea.

"Say, Chao'er — it doesn't have to be human blood, right? Would animal blood do?"

Zhang Chao, purple with strain, blinked. Then, uncertain: "It... it should. Probably."

"Feels like the guy in the coffin... the Boss isn't picky anymore."

"And I don't know why, but I'm real scared of him. Like, scared scared."

There was no time — Zhao Fei missed that last part entirely.

"All right! Animal blood I can handle!"

Then he put on a face of pure delighted surprise, fixed his eyes on the crow overhead, and hollered for all he was worth.

"Bird brother! Bird brother, you came?! We're over here!!"

"Go run and tell Boss Hua and my master — hurry, go — the bad guys are about to kill us!"

Fatty Zhao's bellowing startled the crow — and startled the so-called High Envoy even more.

As the Bone Shaman's trusted subordinate, of course he knew Hua Jiunan.

That was Emperor Tingmeng, the terror that shook the ancient world!

And there was a saying the old survivors passed mouth to mouth, one the High Envoy dared not forget — a rhyme they'd made even the children recite: *Meet Three-Face and you can't tell living from dead; meet Tingmeng and you might as well start digging your own grave.*

Do you remember the Blood-Colored Sea?!

So when the High Envoy heard that the fat crow overhead was an enemy spy, he didn't hesitate for half a heartbeat.

Grinning wickedly, he swept up his staff and loosed a bone arrow at the bird.

A full-power strike from the High Envoy — even the warden couldn't have blocked it head-on. Let alone one "ordinary" crow.

The arrow punched clean through its chest. The crow gave one raw scream and dropped like a stone — a heavy, wet thud, right on the coffin lid.

The blood gushing out of it never even dripped to the ground. The coffin drank every drop, the wood darkening and swelling like a sponge, with a sound like slow swallowing.

What nobody expected was that this crow was anything but ordinary. Dying, its little bead-black eyes bulged with pure hatred, fixed on the High Envoy and Fatty Zhao both, legs still kicking in the air, beak snapping for one last word.

"Son of a — son of a bitch! I just stepped out to find a spot to take a dump and you two set me up?!"

"Just you wait — this ain't over! I'm telling you, this ain't over!"

Then its legs kicked straight out, it gave one last squawk of pure unwillingness, and died.

Zhao Fei: "..."

"Did... did I just screw up?"

"Please tell me that wasn't Feather-brother... Feather-sister's (the Solar Luminary, the little crow Black Feather) relative?!"

But Zhang Chao was at the critical moment and had no time for him.

All anyone heard was him screaming with the last ounce of strength in his body:

"The Northern Dipper governs death, the Southern Dipper governs life! I carry the Jade Emperor's command — I dispatch you to rise and walk!"

"Come out — Boss, Boss Chen!"

And then Zhang Chao stood there, wondering: "Why... why did I call him Boss Chen?"

B.title: 第2297章 人不散（大结局）
B.text:
Time slipped along the way time does when you're young, and before anyone noticed, it was the last winter break of college that Hua Jiunan and Chen Daji would ever share.

Business delayed them, so they didn't make it home until New Year's Day itself, and the sky was already going dark when the train pulled in.

Waiting on the platform — and this was a genuine shock — was Chen Fu, come to meet them himself.

Years had changed Chen Daji. He was steadier now, calmer. But the moment he laid eyes on his father, whom he hadn't seen in ages, all that steadiness evaporated into pure shrieking joy.

"Holy shit — Dad, you're ALIVE? You got out of the chessboard?!"

"Mom's finally a widow no more!"

"One more week stuck in there and I was gonna talk her into remarrying!"

Chen Fu, who had been every bit as thrilled to see his son, apparently decided the train station was as good a place as any for a public demonstration of the principle that spare the rod spoils the child. He beat the little menace soundly, right there in front of everybody.

If Hua Jiunan hadn't physically held him back, father and son, just reunited, would have been parted again on the spot.

From the car came the Big Han's booming laugh as he watched the menace's battered, woebegone face.

Hua Jiunan turned and bowed with a smile, greeting him softly. "Old Ancestor, it's been too long."

The Big Han nodded along, beaming, guileless as a big kid. "Mm-hmm, mm-hmm, far too long!"

"Little Nine, you and Daji both look well... Well, Daji there doesn't look so well. Poor bastard! Hahahaha!"

That Chen fellow came shuffling over too, sniffling.

"Great-gee-grandpa, why didn't you get out of the car and pull my dad off me?"

"Good grief, he nearly beat me to death... So it was YOU who brought him back?"

"Fished him out of that little chessboard?"

At the mention of his own accomplishment, the Big Han's face filled with modest pride. Well — not that modest.

"Darn tooting I did!"

"It wasn't just Chen Fu. I brought everyone back!"

"Except those two old weasels. They wanted divine titles, so Little Nine's mother gave them their official sealing and set them up in the Radiant Lady's mansion."

Only now did the menace remember that his godmother held a whole pantry of divine titles, just waiting to be handed out.

He stuck his thumb up at the Big Han. "A house with an elder in it is a house with a treasure. Old Ancestor, you are the GOAT."

Flattery, delivered in rapid succession, went straight to the old man's head. He nodded like a chicken pecking rice.

"Darn tooting!"

"Didn't I always say it? This Old Ancestor is old, not dead — would I ever let the descendants come up short?!"

"Heh heh!"

Just then, Elder Ghost came walking over with the Yellow Family Ancestor in tow. Neither said a word to the crowd; Elder Ghost spoke only to his own descendant.

"Little Huang, you see how it's done? This is exactly how they beat ME down, back in the day."

"First the small ones gang up on you. Then the big ones."

"And when you finally manage to kill the big ones AND the small ones — out come the old ones."

"The old ones are reasonable enough, I suppose. They won't strike personally. They'll just resurrect the big ones and the small ones, over and over, forever... You tell me how an outsider is supposed to fight that."

Elder Ghost's bitter expression set the whole group laughing.

None of it, of course, was visible to ordinary eyes.

Amid the laughter, Chen Fu drove everyone back to the little courtyard. From far off you could see the New Year couplets pasted on the gate:

*Heaven and earth in harmony, the household flourishing;*

*Peace and good fortune, the whole family reunited.*

The horizontal scroll above read: **ONE HAPPY FAMILY.**

The moment they stepped through the gate, the Master of Wanlong Mountain and Bai Wuwei came out to greet them.

Hua Jiunan stepped forward, and before either of the two household heads could speak: "Brother Bai — you've come home too!"

Bai Wuwei nodded so hard he could barely speak. "By the Human Ancestor's mercy, and through Radiant Lady Guanghua's grace!"

"Little Master — forgive my presumption, but I begged the Lady for a divine title."

"So that I might last a while longer in this world. Read more medical texts. Help more of the poor."

"I acted without permission. Punish me as you see fit."

Hua Jiunan had always been generous with those who served others, and this was the most selfless physician he had ever known. He clapped Bai Wuwei's shoulder three times, smiling.

"There. Sentence carried out."

"Come inside, Brother Bai — don't keep Granny and Nana waiting."

Bai Wuwei's smile turned sly. "Little Master, it isn't only the two elders waiting. General Li has returned as well!"

Meanwhile, that Chen fellow had grabbed Zhang Shizu and was bouncing around him like a puppy.

"Hahaha, Chao'er's great-grandpa, you're alive too?! Did the Old Ancestor fish you back out as well?"

The menace's joy was completely genuine, and it left Zhang Shizu with a mouthful of feelings he didn't know how to swallow. He kept a careful arm's length as he answered, sounding almost wounded.

"Bane of my existence... Young General. This old man's constitution is... special. I didn't need to trouble the Human Ancestor."

"Have you forgotten I'm a Strange Corpse? I climbed back out of the underworld on my own, inch by inch."

"Then I gathered my body back together, piece by piece... and where pieces were missing, I stitched in substitutes. Good enough for government work."

Chen Daji stared. "Ho—holy shit. That WORKS?"

"Chao'er's great-grandpa, level with me. Are you a Transformer or something?"

"You can self-repair?!"

Zhang Shizu and the menace's exchange set off another wave of laughter — and in the middle of it, Hua Jiunan flicked his sleeve. Every flaw in the Ancestor of Corpse-Herders' stitched-together body simply smoothed away, and more than that: a quiet shower of other blessings settled onto the old wonder as well.

Zhang Shizu felt it, and wild joy broke across his face. He dropped to his knees to kowtow in thanks — but Hua Jiunan stopped him with a gesture, and pointed, laughing, at the horizontal scroll on the gate.

Zhang Shizu froze. Then tears welled up in his eyes. "One happy family... Yes. Yes, Little Master. Zhang Shizu understands."

Inside the gate, they found Chang Baye waddling back and forth, helping Chan Third haul stuff around. The moment the little serpent saw Hua Jiunan come in, he tore — well, slithered — across the yard at top speed and shot up onto Hua Jiunan's wrist in a blink.

"Little Master, you're home! Little Eight missed you to DEATH!"

"I-I wanted to go meet you at the train, I really did, but-but Master Chen insisted he'd go."

"Little Eight wasn't going to fight the Squire over it, so I just did chores and waited. That's all I did, just waited."

Hua Jiunan stroked the little serpent's head, his voice gentle. "I know, Eighth Master. It's all right."

As they spoke, the Shameless Cocoon and Grand Warden Xin Lianshan came through the gate flanking Radiant Lady Guanghua and Snow Corpse, one on each side like ceremonial guards.

The warden had finally gotten his wish — a transfer to the Radiant Lady's mansion as the Divine Commander of the Imperial Guard. In the old reckoning that was a proper second-rank official, the kind of post an emperor gave only to his most trusted favorite. Xin Lianshan these days was insufferably pleased with himself.

Spotting Hua Jiunan and Chen Daji, he murmured a request to Snow Corpse, then came wiggling over, big rear end swaying, at the fastest waddle he could manage.

"Hahaha, Little Master, Young General — you're home!"

"Old Xin missed you somethin' fierce!"

"Old Xin's doing just fine, don't you worry about me none!"

The menace grimaced. "Who's worrying about y—"

He never finished. Firecrackers went off in every direction, and everyone froze — then burst out laughing, all together, shouting: "IT'S NEW YEAR!"

And in the middle of the nation's great celebration, Wang San, little Qianyue, and the Fox Maiden came out supporting Deaf Granny and Uncle Li on either arm. Behind them, shy as ever, walked Little Wuxin.

"Namu Amitabha, big brother!"

— Author's afterword: I set down my pen after the last word and couldn't bring myself to lift it again. Every scene of this book passed before my eyes; every old friend crowded my heart. A thousand words rose to my throat and stalled on my lips, until they all condensed into twelve: May the song end but the people never scatter; may every old friend be safe and well. Take care of yourselves, all of you. However high the mountains and long the roads, I believe we will meet again. Thank you for staying to the end — I beg, shamelessly, one last time, for your love and support. My new book *After the Forbidden One* has resumed updates, eight thousand words a day — please give it your support! That Chen fellow, the Dragon Lord Chang Huaiyuan, the Rat Clan Patriarch, Little Wuxin and others will all appear in it, one after another, as legendary figures. Consider it a sequel — the timeline is twenty-two years after this book.

---

**EXTRA: The Stories That Followed**

East of the azure sea, above Guixu — the Abyss of Returning Waters — stood an immortal mountain called Guiqu: Returning Home.

At its summit sat Hua Jiunan, a green qin across his knees, playing the tune "The Moon Sets, the Stars Go Out."

Behind him, eight swords whirled and danced in the air.

Before him, the Fox Maiden moved with the wind, her Rainbow-Feathered Robe gracing the mortal world once more.

Across from him, Auntie Incense Master smiled like a flower and refilled her cup again and again. And behind him — ahem — that Chen fellow was gawking at everything in sight, while the great serpent, a black pot balanced on his head, coiled obediently at Hua Jiunan's feet.

Little Wuxin remained as demure as ever, occasionally peeking up timidly. The moment no one was looking, out came the spicy jerky strips, quickly crammed into his mouth. Then more peeking, more sneaking snacks, more demure murmuring of "Namu Amitabha."

When the song ended, that Chen fellow, who had been holding it in the whole time, finally coughed and spoke up.

"Boss, you play real nice. Fei'er dances real pretty... Auntie Incense Master drinks real fast..."

The Incense Master chuckled. "You rotten boy — if you know I drink fast, why don't you get over here and pour?"

"Coming, coming!" That Chen fellow was always obedient around his elders. He scurried over on his bandy legs like a little lapdog.

"Auntie, is this the Yellow Emperor's wine? I've never had it. Never tasted it. Don't know what it's like. Heh heh!"

The Absolute Sage, the Lady Sovereign, found his cringing manner so funny she laughed all the harder.

"Rotten boy, if you want a drink, just say so. You think your auntie would stop you?"

"Your auntie isn't stingy like certain Old Ancestors I could name."

The Big Han, who had just materialized halfway into view, was caught dead in the middle. If he withdrew now, he'd confirm his stingy reputation; if he stayed, he didn't quite dare talk back to the Incense Master — because she was telling the truth.

While he hung there, frozen, the Jiang Chudi following behind him mercifully failed to brake and bumped him forward. Taking the cue, the Big Han appeared among them, looking sheepish.

Everyone rose at once. "We pay our respects to the Old Ancestor!"

The Big Han waved a hand — everyone carry on, no need for ceremony — then plopped himself down beside the Incense Master.

"Ahem. Xiang'er, it really isn't that I'm stingy. I left in such a hurry I forgot my wine. So I'll just have a bit of yours..."

At this, Jiang Chudi — stout since childhood — showed no reaction at all. But Emperor Zhuanxu, clever since childhood, hurriedly looked down at the ground.

The Incense Master, too wise to argue with the Old Ancestor to his face, just laughed and filled his cup.

Then, half-joking, half-not: "Drink as you please, Old Ancestor."

"But let's agree in advance — you return everything tenfold."

The Big Han froze solid, cup raised, unable to drink it and unable to put it down. His face cycled through several colors before he gave Jiang Chudi's backside a gentle kick.

"You boy — what'd you have to grow so stout for?!"

"If you hadn't bumped me, I — I'd have gone home and gone to bed!"

Emperor Jiang Chu, that lovable tsundere, clearly hadn't followed any of it; his face was pure bafflement. The clever Zhuanxu bowed his head lower still.

But even that wasn't enough to spare him. "What are you smiling at? You've thought of a name for the Grey Clan whelps yet?"

"Let me tell you, that household spawned another hundred-plus litters last month alone!"

As everyone knows, laughter is a migrating species. Except for Zhuanxu, every person on that mountaintop was now laughing.

That Chen fellow chuckled his way cautiously over to the Big Han and kneaded his shoulders with grimy little hands.

"Great-gee-grandpa, you're so domineering, taking it out on other people like that."

"I gotta learn that trick from you!"

"Say, Old Ancestor — could you maybe beat up my dad for me sometime? He keeps beating on me, and I can't beat him back!"

The Big Han doted on that Chen fellow; he roared with laughter. "Darn tooting I will!"

"Oh, right — I like you, boy. Come live with me at the ancestral mountain a few years!"

Chen Daji lit up instantly. "Deal! As long as there's no school, you can put me to anything!"

The very moment he agreed, back at the Ancestral Mountain, the Great Golden Ones were seized by a nameless dread — the sensation of imminent catastrophe. They dropped everything, sat down in perfect unison, closed their eyes, and began divining. They sat down so precisely in sync that the ground itself shuddered. Anyone who didn't know better would have sworn it was a collective fart.

Amid the horseplay, Jiang Chudi asked softly, "Little Nine — the protector of Changsheng was clearly you. So why did the one who fought the final battle turn out to be Wumian?"

It wasn't Hua Jiunan who answered, but Little Wuxin, all bashfulness. The little monk first wiped the chili-oil from his hands — the jerky strips were greasy — then pressed his palms together and bowed.

"Namu Amitabha."

"Big brother took pity on this little monk. Fearing I might not live long, he long ago bound his own life to mine."

"So this little monk is also a protector of Changsheng."

"Ohhh! So that's it!" Jiang Chudi smacked his forehead.

"So in that battle, when Wumian chose to perish together with Changsheng, he cut his own bond to Little Nine first — that's why Little Nine came through unharmed."

"And after that battle, Little Nine spent his own life to pull you back. That's why his hair is white now, though he's still young."

"Namu Amitabha — exactly so. Big brother's mercy is boundless." With that, Little Wuxin ducked shyly behind Hua Jiunan and hid.

Having had his question answered, Emperor Zhuanxu voiced his own worry.

"Little Nine — those two, Bright Heaven and Dark Heaven..."

Hua Jiunan smiled. "Rest easy, uncle. Each keeps to their own office."

"Good!" Zhuanxu nodded deeply. "And those otherworldly flowers cursed by heaven and earth?"

At the mention of the Flower-Spirit and the Leaf-Spirit, Hua Jiunan sighed softly. "Rest easy, uncle. I have arrangements for them too."

"Not only them — Shopkeeper Liu, Xu Fangcao, every one of them has a place to end up."

Seeing that Hua Jiunan had truly left nothing and no one unarranged, Zhuanxu — who had carried the world on his shoulders since before recorded time — finally, fully relaxed.

Just then, another vast pressure rolled across the mountain: a seal and a banner, blotting out the sky. The Command of the Lord of Arms. The Banner of the Lord of Arms.

They circled once overhead, then drifted down to rest upon Hua Jiunan's green qin. From within them came Chiyou's voice — majestic, cold.

"From this day, Tingmeng shall serve as Grand Enforcer of this world in my stead. You will be iron-faced and impartial, without favor, without self."

"Only so will you prove worthy of the name of the True One."

Hua Jiunan hesitated — then picked up the Command and the Banner.

"The True One is without self; the divine is without merit; the sage is without name... Hua Jiunan understands."

"From today, no one at my side may meddle again in the karma of the mortal world. In all things, live as ordinary people."

His voice wasn't loud, but it rang clearly in every ear — wherever in the world that ear happened to be.

On Wanlong Mountain, Chang Huaiyuan and the other four household heads of the medium families bowed low together.

"We obey the Little Master's command!"

The Mohist Sovereign, who had heard it too, wore a face of pure misery. He turned, aggrieved, to Ma Mingyang — the Mohist who was glaring daggers at him — and asked:

"Old Ma. Be honest. Does the Little Master's order cover the two of us?"

Ma Mingyang couldn't be bothered to answer. He simply turned his back — proud, aloof — and said one word: "Guess."

---

**EXTRA: So Many Injustices in This World**

Time galloped, and twenty years went by in a blink. Hua Jiunan was forty now.

Because he had spent his own life to bring Wuxin back, his temples had gone white long ago. But the white hair didn't age him — if anything it gave him the particular charm of a mature man. In the parlance of young women these days: a dad-type. A dad-type overflowing with the hard-won security of the years.

Compared to him, that Chen fellow had changed hardly at all. Age had left a few marks on his face, but not one mark on his character.

It was one in the morning when the wretch tiptoed into Chang Baye's room.

The great serpent — honest, hardworking, dreaming only of earning an honest living for his wife and kids — had spent the whole day planting herbs in the fields and was dead asleep.

That Chen fellow leaned in, wicked as sin, and SCREAMED in his ear.

The serpent nearly convulsed with fright. He shot bolt upright, tail-tip to the floor, standing rigid as a fence post on the heated brick bed, big innocent eyes flickering, enormous head swiveling every which way.

"Who's there?! What happened?!"

"Why'd you scream so awful?!"

"ASSASSINS!"

The word assassin settled it. Without a moment's hesitation he launched himself like a bottle rocket, shot out the window, and streaked straight for Hua Jiunan's room. In the good serpent's heart, his Little Master is always the first thought.

Never mind that the Master was middle-aged now. Never mind that the Master had long since been unbeatable in all three realms.

Yet at Hua Jiunan's door, Chang Baye stopped short.

No sound from inside. That meant the Master was still sleeping.

If the Master was sleeping, there were no assassins. The serpent held it as absolute doctrine that nothing in heaven, earth, or underworld could take Hua Jiunan by surprise — not even the Three Ancestors of the Human Race themselves.

"Master's fine. That's what matters," the great serpent whispered, as quietly as his enormous body allowed. Then he paused.

"Wait. That scream just now... sounded sort of like the little wretch, didn't it?"

"Did the little wretch get assassinated?"

"...Eh. If the little wretch dies, he dies. Honestly, him dying would please me about as much as going home for New Year."

"If he's really dead, there's plenty of time to notify his next of kin tomorrow morning."

Yawning, Chang Baye waddled back toward his own room.

And then Chen Daji's voice, thick with grievance, rose behind him.

"Eighth Master, you hate me THAT much? Rooting for my death that hard?!"

"Even King Yama himself said I should knock off the dying — I'm a burden on the underworld's paperwork!"

"He said if I dare just casually die again, he'll get Brother Ox-Horse and Little-Face Brother to take me out back and beat me in a circle!"

Here the wretch grinned his greasy grin. "Last time I did die and went back, I hid a dynamite cap in Sharp-Beak's rice cooker. You know, Bird Beak, the Underworld Marshal."

"Good grief, the man plugged it in and BOOM."

"Blew his pointy beak clean crooked. He can open beer bottles with it now!"

Chang Baye snorted. "Little wretch, cut the crap. Since when does the underworld have ELECTRICITY? Eighth Master sure never heard about it!"

"What, your daddy the Squire funded a power line down there?"

"Little ghosts turning a millstone to generate it?!"

The wretch looked wounded that he wasn't believed.

"The Squire didn't wire them up — Uncle Zhong and his crew did it themselves, self-reliant!"

"They run the generators on water from the River of Forgetfulness!"

"And to make sure every part of it was done right, Brother Ox-Horse brought a whole mess of experts over from the world of the living ahead of time!"

"Including that one expert — the one who said fresh college grads ought to PAY their employer tuition for the privilege of working!"

"R-really?" Chang Baye was half convinced. "Good. Taking that old bastard was the right call. Man's mean as a snake — talks like he's got no conscience at all."

"His own kid works for somebody, and HE'D want to pay the boss?!"

He paused there, remembering business.

"Little wretch — everything was fine just now. Why'd you scream like that?"

"Good grief, you scared me so bad my vitals ache!"

That Chen fellow — no, he didn't — obviously he wasn't about to admit he'd done it for fun. Otherwise the great serpent would have whipped him into disconnected pieces with that tail.

So he got straight to the point. "Eighth Master, you remember Chan Third?"

"Few days back he was sleeping buck-naked on the ground, and somebody stepped on him. Stepped on him GOOD. Both ends burst."

"He came to me in a dream just now and told me!"

"WHAT?!" Chang Baye's jaw dropped. "Chan Third's a ghost-immortal now! How does somebody STEP on him?!"

"He's a toad — he doesn't even HAVE a vital spot!"

Chen Daji shook his head. "Search me. He didn't say in the dream."

"All he said was get over there and collect his body quick, before the great serpent eats it."

"He wants to be buried whole."

Chang Baye: "......"

But the great serpent was kind at his core. He let Chen Daji climb onto his back at once and point the way. Chan Third wasn't exactly a close friend, but a body couldn't be left to rot in the open wilds.

And besides — a perfectly good big toad, dead under circumstances this unclear? Somebody owed somebody an explanation. If it was deliberate: no discussion needed, the little wretch would punch the killer into next week on Chan Third's behalf. If it was an accident, just somebody passing through — well then, they'd at least apologize to Chan Third proper and watch where they walked next time.

---

**EXTRA: A Child of the Chang Family**

Just as Chang Baye was about to head out, a strange egg drifted out of the room.

(A special note here: this book and *After the Forbidden One* are not the same storyline. Old friends who've read *After the Forbidden One* — bear with us, and no spoilers.)

This was Chang Baye's son. The son he'd had with the Ying Dragon, named Chang Jie.

Only — like our Eighth Master — the boy had been born with a weak constitution, and had hatched only halfway. Top half out. Bottom half still stuck in the shell.

Seen from a distance, he looked exactly like a rotten egg crawling with maggots.

And that maggot had mismatched eyes — one big, one small, both cross-eyed — crowned by two ferociously thick eyebrows. There was no angle from which the boy did not look profoundly wrong.

Chang Jie came drifting out this way, slow as a balloon with no wind in it, grumbling all the while in heartbroken tones.

"Both my parents are dragons... and I'm a maggot. Where in the world is the justice..."

Before Chang Baye could open his mouth, the Young General had already scampered over and scooped the boy up — whereupon Chang Jie resisted, planting rapid little kisses all over the wretch's fleshy head until it was dripping.

"Aww, Little Jie, it's the middle of the night — what're you doing out?"

"Tummy upset? You gotta go poop?"

The poor little maggot hung in the Young General's arms wearing the expression of a man with nothing left to live for.

Chang Baye snapped his tail and sent that Chen fellow flying, then caught his precious darling in one smooth motion and said nearly the same thing himself: "Little Jie, you're frail. What are you doing up at this hour?"

"Listen to your daddy. Go back to bed."

"Missing your mama, can't sleep? Where'd Old Diplomas put your pacifier?"

"Suck on it a while and you'll drop right off. There's a good boy."

"Okay." Chang Jie's voice was boneless with exhaustion. He nodded and drifted back toward the house, grumbling as he went. "Both my parents are dragons... and I'm a maggot. Where is the justice..."

He drifted very slowly. Halfway there, he stopped — and turned around.

Chang Baye was curious. "Little Jie? What now? Weren't we going back to bed?"

Chang Jie sighed. "Dad, the Young General was right. My stomach IS upset. I was going to the toilet."

"You two interrupted me and I forgot."

"Oh! Oh, of course!" Chang Baye nodded rapidly. "Go on then, go!"

"You scared? Scared, Daddy will come with you."

"You bring paper? Bring the soft kind, remember."

"You're too tender down there — the hard stuff'll chafe you."

As Chang Baye rattled on with fatherly concern, what little life remained in Chang Jie's face guttered and went dark. He said nothing. He simply turned and drifted back inside, sighing with every foot of the way, as though the world no longer held a single thing worth staying for.

Seeing his son like this, Chang Baye panicked.

"Little Jie?! What's wrong? Did Daddy do something wrong?"

"Or are you not feeling well?"

Chang Jie knew how deeply his father loved him, and for once answered at speed — instead of his usual glacial pace that could make a saint tear his hair out.

"Daddy, don't worry. It's a small problem."

"I had to poop, then I forgot, then you held me up — and I went in the shell."

"So no toilet needed. I'll just go back inside and wash my bottom."

Chang Baye: "......"

"Good boy. I'm so sorry, son..."

By then the tail-launched Chen Daji had limped back into view. "Ow, ow, OW — Eighth Master, you're getting stronger!"

"It's only me! Anybody else you'd have whipped into confetti!"

Chang Baye, still thoroughly sick of his best frenemy, sniffed coldly.

"I don't whip other people. Only whip you, you little wretch."

"Now quit dawdling and sit there like a good boy."

"Eighth Master's going to bathe Little Jie first. Then we go collect Chan Third's body."

All the commotion naturally woke the Master. A lamp lit, and Hua Jiunan's voice came through the door, as gentle as ever: "Eighth Master, Daji — what's wrong? Is there something you need my help with?"

The honest serpent shook his head so hard his head wobbled like a rattle-drum, the 'tongue' of the pot on it flapping.

"No, no, Little Master, it's a small thing."

"So sorry to disturb your rest! Little Eight was wrong!"

With Chang Baye, the Master could only be gentler still.

"Eighth Master, why are you always so formal with me?"

"You didn't disturb anything. Really, I'm going back to sleep — you and Daji don't stay up too late."

"And Little Jie especially — it's cold out, don't let him go outside... Actually — is he scared to sleep alone? Bring him here. I'll tell him stories until he's off."

Chang Jie had grown up in the Master's arms. The Master had held him and soothed him to sleep more hours than his own parents ever had. Of everyone in the world, Chang Jie was closest to the Master.

And the Master's doting on Chang Jie was, quite simply, unprecedented and unrivaled.

For the boy's first birthday, the Master summoned the God of Fortune, the God of Wealth, the God of Joy — every auspicious deity there was — to bestow blessings on the child. Beyond the gods, the Old Ancestor arrived leading all of the Great Golden Ones. The great Kuafu the Sun-Chaser, the goddess Meng Po, an uninvited Chiyou the Lord of Arms, and the Fengdu Emperor at the head of the Five Ghost Emperors of the Directions with the entire senior staff of the underworld...

Put it this way: the sealing ceremony for this one child took over an hour. measured against Chang Baye's own sealing, back in the day, it was heaven and earth.

And even so, Chang Jie remained a "maggot."

If the Master hadn't sworn to his face that one day the boy would ring out with a dragon's roar that shook the ninth heaven and moved the whole earth with a single motion — Chang Jie would have gone and found a glass marble to dash his brains out on, then and there.

One special note: strange as the boy looks, he is frighteningly clever. At one year old he had the brains of an eighteen-year-old — and not just any eighteen-year-old; one of the ones who gets into the top universities in the country.
